summary: None of the three upstream funders return what their raw response looks like it returns — NIH RePORTER matches machine-generated concept tags and emits one row per support year rather than per project, NSF matches anywhere in the abstract and orders by recency, and Grants.gov leaves opportunities in 'posted' status indefinitely — so each source needs a client-side relevance, dedup and recency layer: NIH must restrict search_field to title and abstract, whitelist applicable activity codes, send the amount floor as a request criterion, request core_project_num and over-fetch and dedup on it keeping the highest-amount support year, and report a threshold-probed median plus counts described as award records rather than awards; NSF must pool several pages, require every query term by stem, deduplicate collaborative re-registrations by normalised title and rank title hits above abstract hits; Grants.gov must request sortBy openDate|desc, report absent and placeholder close dates as unstated rather than rolling, and flag results posted more than two years ago.
reason: NIH concept tags: the 'terms' field is attached to every project independently of its subject, so a building management award matches a disease keyword and outranks real research on amount. Activity codes must be filtered server-side because the API accepts the criterion and a client-side pass would discard most of each page. The amount floor cannot be applied after the fact: the API returns the largest awards first, so a post-filter only removes rows and never pulls smaller matching awards into view. The median must be located by counting awards above a series of thresholds rather than by sampling a page, because the distribution is heavily right-skewed and any single page is a biased slice. max_amount must also stay below 2,147,483,647: above it RePORTER returns an empty-body HTTP 500 that is indistinguishable from an outage. NIH support years: measured on 100 records the API returned 71 distinct projects, and core project 5R01CA092447 alone occupied 11 rows; in the top 15 rows sorted by award amount only 7 distinct projects were present, so the size-sorted listing a user actually reads was more than half duplicates. Truncating the full project number is not a valid dedup key: observed forms 5R01CA092447-08, 2R01CA092447-06A1 and 3R01CA092447-08S1 vary in both the leading application-type digit and the suffix length, so no fixed-width truncation works; the API already returns core_project_num, it was simply missing from the response struct. NSF: one page of results for 'quantum computing' is dominated by awards whose ~2,900-character abstract mentions the phrase once in boilerplate, and the genuinely on-topic awards sit below the page boundary where no client-side filter can reach them; stem matching is required because abstracts say 'resilient' where the user typed 'resilience'; dedup must key on the normalised title, not the award ID, because collaborative awards are registered once per institution with distinct IDs. Grants.gov: measured 2026-08-11 for the keyword 'climate', of 66 posted results the first row was a NOAA call opened in July 2011 for fiscal year 2012, 8 predated 2022, 19 carried an empty closeDate and 2 carried the placeholder 01/01/2099; sorting rather than filtering is deliberate — the API's dateRange parameter cuts the same 66 results to 27 at one year and 7 at 30 days, which would discard genuinely rolling programs such as a 2020 posting that runs to 2030, and openDateFrom is accepted by the API and has no effect on the hit count, so it must not be used in place of sortBy. A regen that restores search_field=all, drops the NIH activity code whitelist, estimates the NIH median from returned rows, drops core_project_num or the over-fetch factor or restores wording that calls the API total 'matching awards', restores a single NSF keyword request or an exact-string filter over it, or drops the Grants.gov sort key, reintroduces results that look like a funder data problem rather than a client one.
validated_outcome: NIH concept tags and award types — FY2024 'cancer' sorted by award: largest result fell from $366,260,951 (a library services project) to $2,833,086, and grants an external applicant can compete for rose from 1 of the top 25 to 25 of 25; reported typical award $450,000 in the $400,000-$500,000 bracket, matching an independent threshold probe of the API, while sampling the 300 smallest matching rows instead gave $34,465. NIH support years — with core_project_num requested, nihOverFetch = 6 and dedup keeping the highest-amount support year per core project, a 15-row listing went from 7 distinct projects to 15 distinct projects. NSF — six pooled pages vs one page, counting awards containing every term: gene therapy 2 -> 34 (11 title hits), artificial intelligence 18 -> 115 (21), climate resilience 2 -> 6 (2). Grants.gov — keyword 'climate', first page: every one of the top 8 results now opened in 2026 and carries a real deadline, against a 2011 record in first place before the change; at --rows 60 the CLI reports '23 of 60 shown were posted over two years ago' and marks each with its posting date.
